abstract: ECOSIMULATE presents a web-based air-quality monitoring and mitigation simulation prototype. The system combines live air-quality observations, a custom Pollution Index and virtual urban grids to explore hypothetical artificial-tree deployment scenarios. Implemented using Python Flask and interactive web visualization, the prototype supports city-level monitoring and scenario comparison. The reported reductions are simulation outputs, rather than independently measured intervention effects. The study identifies field validation, expanded environmental inputs and predictive modelling as future work.
title: ECOSIMULATE: Pollution Mitigation and Simulation using AI-Driven Environmental Modeling
content:
## Research motivation

Urban air pollution monitoring alone cannot communicate how hypothetical interventions might change local environmental conditions. ECOSIMULATE integrates live air-quality information with an interactive, equation-based framework for exploring artificial-tree deployment scenarios. Its implemented contribution is a simulation prototype, not a field-validated treatment or a trained forecasting model.

## Research objectives

- Integrate air-quality observations from an external API into a city-level monitoring interface.
- Represent urban areas using virtual grids and calculate a custom Pollution Index (PI).
- Allow users to vary artificial-tree density and inspect modelled intervention scenarios.
- Provide a basis for further environmental modelling and researcher-oriented analysis.

## Data acquisition and system architecture

The paper describes seven monitoring locations: Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Chennai, Pune, Munnar and Manali. Data ingestion retrieves air-quality observations using the Google Air Quality API. The paper also describes meteorological inputs and processing steps for unit normalization, missing-data handling and fallback to the last successful response.

| Layer | Implementation described in the paper |
| --- | --- |
| Data ingestion | Google Air Quality API; JSON processing |
| Data processing | Python, normalization and fallback handling |
| Simulation | Custom equation; virtual grids of approximately 23,000 square metres |
| Backend | Python Flask |
| Frontend | HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript |
| Visualization | Plotly.js and Leaflet.js |
| Researcher access | Basic authentication and advanced simulation controls |

The prototype was hosted locally. Cloud migration and trained machine learning forecasting were proposed extensions, rather than established deployment or forecasting results.

## Mathematical formulation

The paper defines a weighted score using temperature, particulate matter, carbon monoxide and artificial-tree count. It describes constraining the score to the interval from 0 to 100. An explicit interpretation of that stated constraint is:

$$
S = 0.3T + 0.4PM + 1.2CO - 0.8AT
$$

$$
PI = \min(100,\max(0,S))
$$

Here $T$ denotes temperature in degrees Celsius, $PM$ denotes PM2.5 concentration in micrograms per cubic metre, $CO$ denotes carbon monoxide in parts per million, and $AT$ denotes the number of artificial trees per grid.

The displayed clipping equation makes the paper's stated bounds explicit; the paper itself prints a less fully specified minimum expression. These coefficients define an assumed simulation score, not a physically calibrated atmospheric transport model, and the custom PI is not the official regulatory AQI.

## Reported simulation scenarios

The paper reports the following Delhi-grid scenario comparison (Figure 5, Results and Discussion). The values and percentage annotations below are reproduced as reported scenario outputs; they are not field measurements of intervention effectiveness.

| Scenario | PM2.5 (µg/m³) | NO2 (µg/m³) | AQI |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Baseline | 95 | 50 | 240 |
| 100 trees | 65 (31.6% lower) | 32 (36% lower) | 180 |
| 50 trees + traffic control | 58 (38.9% lower) | 28 (44% lower) | 162 |

The paper separately describes approximately 30% average PI reduction in a simulated 50-tree scenario. The comparison table reports pollutant and AQI outputs; it is not an independently validated conversion of the custom PI equation into pollutant concentrations. Traffic control is a combined scenario, so its reported difference cannot be attributed to trees alone.

## Interpretation and limitations

The prototype demonstrates an interactive mechanism for exploring scenario assumptions, not empirical evidence that a given number of artificial trees will deliver the displayed pollution reduction. The paper acknowledges uniform assumed absorption efficiency, omission of dynamic emissions, simplified meteorology, limited pollutant coverage in the equation, API availability constraints and local deployment. Site-specific field measurements and calibration would be necessary to establish actual intervention effects.

## Research evolution

ECOSIMULATE established the simulation and monitoring foundation for subsequent work on AQI forecasting. Veridian investigates comparative machine learning forecasting under chronological evaluation, while AeroCausal is a planned investigation of causal attribution under explicit identification assumptions. These are separate research questions: hypothetical intervention scenarios, future prediction and causal estimation.
